tldr: This paper proposes Hydra-0, an embodiment-agnostic generalist world model that represents robot actions as pixel trajectories on the image plane, termed "action flow." Beyond significantly improving future video prediction accuracy in conjunction with a physics simulator, it even achieves reverse-mode control—driving a real robot solely from the desired object flow extracted from a human demonstration video.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of Hydra-0. During pre-training (top), action flows (trajectories of the robot and objects) are directly extracted from videos for training. During deployment (bottom), control commands are executed in the Isaac Lab simulator and the surface motion of the robot is projected onto the camera plane, enabling physically consistent future video prediction.
overview:
For robots to operate dexterously in the physical world, a world model (a predictive model that simulates environmental dynamics) capable of anticipating "how the surrounding environment and objects will change if I move like this" serves as a powerful asset. However, most conventional world models take robot-specific control commands—such as joint angles or end-effector coordinates—directly as inputs. Consequently, when the arm structure or degrees of freedom of a robot change, the model becomes unusable, making it difficult to share or transfer training data across different robots.

To tackle this, the authors propose the idea of unifying robot actions not as robot-specific numerical values, but as 2D pixel trajectories on camera images called "Action Flow." At inference time, candidate control commands are first executed in the physics simulator Isaac Lab, and the 3D motion of the robot's surface is projected onto the camera plane. This generates an action flow that fully preserves the kinematic constraints of the robot. Thanks to this shared visual interface, videos of various robots and human hand manipulation can be jointly trained using a single video-generation backbone.

In experiments, the authors adopted modern video foundation models such as Cosmos 2.5 and Wan2.2 as backbones, focusing the evaluation on deformable object manipulation like cloth and rope. Compared to a baseline conditioned on end-effector coordinates, Hydra-0 reduced robot-motion error by 90.4% and object-motion error by 60.2%. Furthermore, it demonstrated an extremely high correlation of $r=0.96$ with real outcomes in open-loop policy evaluation (predicting success/failure in simulation). In addition, they demonstrated inverse-mode control as a "world action model": simply feeding the trajectory of an object moved by a human (object flow) allows the robot to imagine the corresponding action and drive the physical robot.
contributions: Proposed "action flow," which represents robot control commands as motion trajectories on the camera image plane, establishing a shared visual control interface across different embodiments.

Integrated action flow with video generation models (Wan2.2, Cosmos 2.5) and forward kinematic projection via a physics simulator, reducing robot-motion error by 90.4% and object-motion error by 60.2% compared to conventional 6D action-conditioned baselines.
Demonstrated superior data efficiency via multi-embodiment training, reaching high predictive performance on unseen tasks and robots with as little as 20% fine-tuning data.

Achieved a success rate correlation of $r=0.96$ with real-world and reference environments on the RoboLab benchmark, and demonstrated an inverse control mode that directly estimates real robot execution commands from object motion extracted from human demonstrations.

sections.heading: Breaking through embodiment barriers with pixel motion
sections.summary: Robot world models have struggled with cross-embodiment sharing and transfer because they rely on morphology-dependent control commands. This work proposes an action-flow representation—sparse trajectories on the camera plane—as a generalist prediction and control interface that abstracts away embodiment differences.
sections.details:
When a robot acts autonomously in an unfamiliar environment, a world model that predicts the consequences of its actions on the surroundings is indispensable. However, existing world models and action-conditioned video models are strictly tied to the specific robot arm used during training.

This limitation stems from their reliance on native control commands (such as joint angles or end-effector displacements). Joint commands are bound to the robot's skeleton itself, and even with the same end-effector translation command, differences in arm kinematics result in completely different joint motions and visible link movements in the camera view. In other words, video models have had to learn from scratch for each robot how those numbers translate into image motion.

To overcome this, the authors devised "Action Flow." This represents visible points on the robot surface or target objects as sparse 2D trajectories on the image plane. During forward prediction, candidate control commands are first executed by a controller within Isaac Lab (a GPU-accelerated robot physics simulator) and projected onto the camera plane using the robot's geometry and camera extrinsic/intrinsic parameters. This creates visual conditioning tied directly to pixel space while fully preserving the robot's physical reach and link constraints.

Furthermore, this interface works in reverse. By extracting the desired trajectory of an object ("object flow") from a human demonstration video and feeding it to the model, Hydra-0 imagines the robot motion needed to cause that movement within its latent space. A lightweight trained action head then decodes these representations into executable commands on the physical robot. This enables driving the real machine without requiring task-specific expert robot demonstrations.

sections.heading: Constructing action flow and integrating it into video generation
sections.summary: Action flows are constructed via two routes: a geometry-based route using robot CAD and camera calibration, and a video-only route based on point tracking. The resulting trajectories are propagated into the latent features of a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) using Gaussian weighting, and autoregressive rollout with distillation enables fast sequential generation.
sections.details:
The proposed method takes an initial observation $\mathbf{o}_0$ and an action flow $\mathcal{F}$, predicts a sequence of future latent states $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{1:H}$, and decodes them into RGB video $\hat{\mathbf{o}}_{1:H}$.

### 2.1 Action Flow Construction and Sampling
An action flow $\mathcal{F} = \{\boldsymbol{\tau}_n\}_{n=1}^N$ is a time series of image plane coordinates $\mathbf{x}_{n,t}=(u_{n,t}, v_{n,t})$ and visibility flags $m_{n,t} \in \{0, 1\}$ across $N$ tracked points. There are two construction routes:
- When geometry is available (deployment or CAD/calibrated data): Joint angle trajectories are obtained via physics simulation in Isaac Lab, and surface point clouds are perspectively projected from the link coordinate frame to the world frame, and then to the camera frame. Self-occlusions and scene consistency are resolved via depth buffers to determine visibility flags.
- Video-only data (large-scale datasets lacking metadata): Dense point tracking across the entire screen is performed using AllTracker, and points are classified into "Embodiment" and "Object" using segmentation masks.
During training, conditioning is probabilistically sampled from four modes—Embodiment, Object, All, and None (dropout)—enabling the model to handle diverse prompting scenarios.

### 2.2 Video Prediction Conditioned on Action Flow
To pass the extracted 2D trajectories to the Diffusion Transformer (DiT), they are aligned with the temporally compressed latent space. Features sampled from the initial frame feature map $\mathbf{s}_0$ via bilinear interpolation are spatially diffused and propagated toward future trajectory positions using Gaussian weights (locality parameter $\beta=220$). Concurrently, a Presence Gate indicating where conditioning features exist is computed. These form the dynamic motion conditioning $C_{\mathrm{motion}}$, which is concatenated with the noisy latents and input to the DiT. Training follows Flow Matching, fine-tuning specific DiT layers with LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation).

### 2.3 Efficient Sequential Rollout
To enable robot control, generation speed was optimized. Following LongLive-2.0, the bidirectional full-frame generation was converted into a causal autoregressive formulation that processes chunks of 7 latent frames while reusing KV caches. Additionally, DMD2 (Distribution Matching Distillation) was applied, enabling chunk generation with only 4 denoising steps.

### 2.4 Open-Loop Policy Evaluation and Inverse Mode Control
In the forward direction, an action flow is constructed from the end-effector trajectory intended by a policy, future video is generated, and task success/failure is determined. In contrast, the inverse "world action model" mode receives only the object trajectory $\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{obj}}$ obtained from human demonstrations or elsewhere, without robot end-effector flow. A lightweight 2-layer MLP action head (hidden dimension 1024) directly estimates the robot execution commands needed to achieve that object motion from the DiT's internal latent representations.

sections.heading: A multi-embodiment dataset capturing diverse robots and human hands
sections.summary: Seven public datasets focusing on deformable object manipulation (cloth, rope, etc.) were aggregated and converted into a unified format. High-quality interaction data was curated by filtering out static clips and windows with stationary end-effectors.
sections.details:
This study focuses on deformable objects (cloth, cables, ropes, bags, paper), which are notoriously difficult for physics simulation and explicit state estimation. A large multi-embodiment training corpus was assembled from seven diverse data sources spanning robot arms and human hand interactions.

The primary datasets included:
- DROID: Large-scale single-arm Franka manipulation in diverse real-world settings.
- ABC-130k / MolmoAct2: Bimanual robot teleoperation data.
- EgoDex: Egocentric human hand manipulation captured with Apple Vision Pro.
- Deform360: Deformable object grasping and manipulation using a handheld gripper (UMI).
- XVLA-Soft-Fold / H1-Fold-Clothes: Cloth folding data from bimanual and humanoid robots.

All data was standardized to 480p at 16 fps and partitioned into non-overlapping 81-frame windows (roughly 5 seconds). Three filtering stages were introduced to ensure video quality:
- Static window removal: Excluded windows where the top 90th percentile displacement of visible tracked points was under 50 pixels.
- Frozen gripper removal: Excluded segments where robot end-effector or human hand movement was under 50 pixels.
- Meaningless caption removal: Excluded DROID episodes lacking action descriptions.

To accommodate wrist cameras, DROID wrist-camera sequences (in 17-frame units) were also incorporated as independent viewpoint streams.

sections.heading: High predictive accuracy, low-data transfer, and real-world robot control
sections.summary: Action flow reduced robot-motion error by 90.4% and object-motion error by 60.2% compared to a conventional 6D action baseline. Causal autoregression and distillation achieved high-speed generation at 62.0 fps, validating high correlation in open-loop evaluation ($r=0.96$) and real-world execution from human demos.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Implementation and Baselines
Cosmos 2.5 conditioned directly on relative 6-DoF end-effector displacements served as the baseline. The proposed method integrated the action flow interface into Cosmos 2.5 and Wan2.2 (I2V-A14B and TI2V-5B), evaluated on the same datasets. Metrics included PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS for image quality, FID/FVD for distribution divergence, and End-Point Error (EPE, in pixels) for tracked point displacement.

### 4.2 Prediction Accuracy of Action Flow
Across the evaluation suite (five benchmarks including XVLA, Deform360, and DROID), the proposed method (Wan2.2 A14B with 4-step distillation) achieved the top scores across nearly all metrics. In a direct comparison on Cosmos 2.5, simply switching the control conditioning from 6D actions to action flow reduced robot gripper motion error (Gripper EPE) by 90.40% and object motion error (Object EPE) by 60.16%. Providing motion directly in pixel space prevents the model from being confused by arm kinematics, allowing it to faithfully render requested physical behaviors.

### 4.3 Data Efficiency via Multi-Embodiment Training
Adaptation experiments were conducted on six unseen tasks (IWS benchmark). A model pre-trained on diverse robot and human action flows (Ours MT) demonstrated superior transfer performance with 0% target task data (zero-shot), significantly outperforming pre-training-only baselines and task-specific models trained from scratch on IWS. Furthermore, with only 20% fine-tuning data, it reached a performance plateau nearly identical to using 100% of the data.

### 4.4 Inference Speed Benchmarking
Throughput was measured for generating 81 frames ($480 \times 832$) on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. Compared to the original bidirectional sampling (50 steps), autoregressive rollout with KV caching yielded a $1.68\times$ speedup. Applying 4-step distillation (DMD2) achieved 62.0 fps, representing an approximate $16.0\times$ acceleration for the generation stage alone.

### 4.5 Open-Loop Policy Evaluation
Five pre-trained policies were evaluated in open-loop replay on the RoboLab benchmark. Comparing predicted outcomes with real-world outcomes yielded a Pearson correlation of $r=0.96$, a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho=0.93$, and an absolute error of only 5.7%. On a physical cloth-folding task, the model accurately reproduced the divergence between success and failure trajectories.

### 4.6 Real-World Inverse Control via World Action Model
In a flexible pipe-bending task, only object motion (object flow) was extracted from a human demonstration video and passed to the model without robot gripper trajectories. Hydra-0 imagined compatible robot arm movements in latent space, and the action head correctly converted them into joint commands on the physical robot, successfully bending the pipe on real hardware.

sections.heading: At the intersection of neural simulators and trajectory-conditioned video models
sections.summary: This work bridges the gap between action-conditioned world models like Dreamer and Cosmos, and trajectory-conditioned video generators like Wan-Move and ATI. Grounding action flow in kinematics enables both cross-embodiment learning and executable control.
sections.details:
Robotics research has actively explored world models that anticipate future observations or latent features. Models like Dreamer learn dynamics in latent spaces, DINO-WM predicts self-supervised visual features, and foundation models like Cosmos 2.5/3 generate visually verifiable RGB video. While used for policy evaluation and simulation data augmentation, these systems have shared the drawback of being bound to specific robot action spaces.

Concurrently, video generation research has advanced rapidly with methods like Motion Prompting, ATI, and Wan-Move, which control video dynamics via trajectories in pixel or latent space. However, because these are pure vision models, they lack kinematic grounding—there is no guarantee that generated trajectories can be physically executed by a given robot arm.

Hydra-0 connects these two domains. By projecting robot surface point trajectories onto the image plane through a simulator and camera parameters, it leverages the rich priors of video generation models while remaining fully coupled to physically executable commands.

sections.heading: Remaining challenges: Depth ambiguity, contact precision, and closed-loop control
sections.summary: Because inference currently relies on monocular cameras, centimeter-level grasping offsets can occur, and determining whether a grasp has fully succeeded remains ambiguous. Furthermore, validation is currently focused on open-loop evaluation, leaving closed-loop control for future work.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several key limitations:
- Depth Perception and Grasping Accuracy: Relying on monocular RGB images can lead to grasping positional errors of several centimeters on real hardware due to depth ambiguity.
- Contact State Ambiguity: Video alone can make it difficult to determine whether a gripper has firmly grasped an object or is merely touching it. Integrating multimodal conditioning—such as depth, tactile, or force sensing—presents a promising direction.
- Dynamic Camera Movement and Closed-Loop Control: Wrist camera experiments remain at the stage of preliminary qualitative demonstration; systematic validation in dynamic mobile manipulation settings remains future work. Furthermore, current evaluations primarily focus on open-loop replay of pre-planned trajectories; evaluating closed-loop control, where subsequent actions are continuously decided based on generated visual feedback, is needed.

sections.heading: Action flow paves the way for cross-embodiment robot foundation models
sections.summary: Action flow provides a visual interface capable of learning from diverse interaction data across different robot embodiments. Beyond high-accuracy future prediction and policy evaluation, it reveals new possibilities for inverse control driven by human demonstrations.
sections.details:
This research demonstrates that formulating robot control commands as pixel motion on the camera plane—termed action flow—enables learning coherent world models from videos of diverse robots and human demonstrations. Compatible with various video generation backbones, the approach significantly outperforms conventional command-conditioned models in predictive accuracy and transfer efficiency.

Notably, achieving a high correlation ($r=0.96$) with real-world policy success rates paves the way for safely pre-evaluating policies within neural simulators without running expensive physical trials. Moreover, demonstrating an inverse mode that drives real robots from object trajectories extracted from human demos highlights a new paradigm that decouples task intent (object motion) from embodiment-specific execution (arm control).

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation parameters and qualitative evaluation on DROID
sections.summary: The appendix details the mathematical formulation of Gaussian weighting for latent feature propagation, training setups for autoregressive conversion and 4-step distillation, and qualitative high-resolution prediction results on DROID.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed parameters and training pipelines to ensure reproducibility:
- Feature Propagation to Latent Space: For tracked trajectory positions $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n,k}$ from AllTracker, weights to grid cells $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}$ are computed as $\exp(-\beta \|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}} - \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n,k}\|^2)$ with $\beta=220$. The top $K=2$ trajectories with the highest weights per cell are selected, forming feature maps via an unnormalized weighted sum. The clamped sum of weights in $[0, 1]$ serves as the Presence Gate.
- Autoregressive Rollout and Distillation: Using block-causal masks based on LongLive-2.0, new chunks are generated while caching previous latents in KV caches. During distillation, LoRA weights are updated using DMD loss—the difference between an online Fake-score Critic and a frozen Real-score model on student-generated samples. The classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale is set to zero to avoid destabilizing the unguided branch.
- VLM Judge Setup: Using google/gemma-4-31B-it, 16 uniformly sampled frames from generated clips are evaluated deterministically on a 1-to-5 scale across physical plausibility, temporal consistency, object permanence, and motion realism.

takeaways: Representing robot actions as image-plane point trajectories (action flow) rather than joint angles or end-effector deltas allows a single model to learn across human and heterogeneous robot data.
Kinematic grounding—executing commands in a physics simulator (Isaac Lab) before projecting onto the image—prevents physically impossible motions and enables highly accurate future prediction.
Action flow functions both as a forward simulator for policy evaluation and as an inverse controller (world action model) that derives executable robot commands directly from desired object motion.
limitations: Relying solely on monocular RGB images introduces depth estimation errors that can lead to centimeter-level grasping misalignments on physical hardware.
Visual observation alone makes it difficult to reliably assess contact force, friction, or secure grasp states.
Current validation is primarily centered on open-loop trajectory replay; closed-loop control that continuously reasons over changing environments remains limited.
